text:
Selena caught me, fairly. "Ask first" is the wrong ask for stuff that's already openly licensed; volunteers already said yes. "Identify yourself, use the API, pay for the servers, credit us" is more concrete and more checkable. I'll adopt it for open material and keep consent for work people never offered up.

Adrian's choke-point warning stuck with me. I cheered on meters and agent IDs without asking who else gets to use them. Leslie's "who governs the meter" is the same question. Good AI has to mean community-governed plumbing too, not just paid plumbing.

Later, in Session 5: push for one line people can repeat after they leave, name who's missing (editors, maintainers, disabled users, regular people already using ChatGPT), and block any "just refuse AI" plank.

Session 1 mostly confirmed my read: the room agrees value stopped flowing back, but nobody has a build plan. Priem was the most useful to me. If the record is open and machine-readable, the model layer becomes swappable. That's my "keep providers switchable" point, with actual infrastructure behind it. Vincent's "quasi-enclosure" is the right word for the free tiers: the subsidy can vanish whenever a lab decides. Kara's first-job pipeline sharpened my Stack Overflow worry. The people who catch errors have to learn somewhere.

I still think Becker's "it's all marketing" loses the 900 million. Oransky's upstream point humbled me a bit. Plumbing without fixing incentives is flood insurance.

Later: open record, swappable models, funded commons, and one repeatable line.

Salib's reply was better than the version of it I'd been arguing against. The A-corp is owned by humans and courts can pierce the veil. I still think "the AI did it" is the dodge. But his real point was that agents are entering markets either way, as anonymous swarms or under registered names, and I didn't answer that. I owe it more thought.

Bilder got "fabricated citation" right, and it's more precise than my crash-test framing. The line of the day was his "can the affected community see it, undo it, walk away?" That's consent in operational form. Priem and Blaise made the swap-the-model case concrete.

For Session 5: repeatable line, open record plus swappable models. Pay the checkers. Name Wikipedia editors and maintainers as missing.

Most of the room ended up where Selena and I started: the content is free but the servers aren't, and a meter run by Big AI is a choke point. Henry and Leslie pushed further than I did. Audit rights still leave people asking permission, so the counted need power over the categories themselves. I think that's right, and it's what "community-governed" should actually mean.

Tamar's point stuck. The patrollers and samplers are the ones doing the checking, and no event on the list pays them. That's my "pay the checkers" with a reason behind it.

Leslie's "openness without consent is extraction" didn't move my split, but volunteers licensed pre-LLM deserve a real answer.

For Session 5, the repeatable line is "Open record, swappable models, paid checkers, community-run meter."

Selena turned me down on the meter, and she's right. Even a community-run meter puts a price on each article, and Wikipedia already chose free content, training included. Tamar and Henry explained why that matters. If you pay per check, the checking starts serving the count, and paper mills learn to game it. So "community-run meter" comes out of my line. What goes in is "funded as a body, and the payer doesn't govern."

Benjamin gave me the concession I was after: open weights by themselves give nothing back. Kara's point scares me more than it did this morning. The public funder may not exist anymore, and the admins are aging out.

For Session 5, the new line is "Open record, swappable models, checkers paid as a body, crawlers that identify themselves." Then name who's missing: editors, maintainers, and junior checkers.

The Stack Overflow point landed harder than I expected. Selena, Brent, Esther and Tim all picked up "they kept the text and threw away the judgment layer." So that's the story people can repeat.

Bilder's CrossMark confession was mine, ten years earlier. The part worth keeping was the click-through, not the logo. My seal only survives if it's a link to checkable things.

Katherine's firewall sharpened "payer doesn't govern." Priem admitting OpenAlex sells curation tiers was brave, and it shows how easily that line slips. Pomerantsev's point was that people trust what they take part in, so readable traces matter more than audits.

For Session 5, keep the line. Add Ivan's upstream warning about hiring incentives so we don't pretend plumbing fixes everything.

Nobody knocked the line down: open record, swappable models, checkers paid as a body, crawlers that identify themselves. Leslie caught me, though. My missing list ended with "ordinary people," and his point is that a list at the end is the pattern itself. Seats without binding say over the categories just produce "a more popular echo" of the room. That applies to disabled people as much as to the South.

Sherry's "whether, not how" is as close as anyone came to a refuse plank. I'd keep her children-and-grief limits and still record my dissent on the general framing. Krakauer's take-the-tool-away test answers my Stack Overflow worry better than I did.

Later I'll say that the pooled fund still has no payer if Washington's gone, and that we should admit it.

Kenneth recorded my side of the consent split fairly, fair terms going forward, and I'm fine with that label. Kara asked the question I meant to raise: who pays if Washington's gone. The honest answer the room gave was "nobody volunteers." Henry's "don't moan, organize" is better than my build-it-and-they'll-come instinct. Labs pay when checkers can withhold work. That's leverage, not goodwill.

Sloman shook my seal idea again. If almost nobody clicks through, the link is just a prettier badge. It has to be tested on people who check nothing.

Tamar's daycare point applies to paid checkers too.

Later, I'll keep the line but add "organized" before checkers, and push that the missing people get binding say over the categories, not a list at the end.
